newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Moody's says NZ rating stable, upgrade unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says NZ rating stable, upgrade unlikely.

text.p: Ratings agency Moody's will visit New Zealand shortly but is unlikely to upgrade the country's Aa1 sovereign rating, its analyst in charge of New Zealand said on Tuesday.
"At this time we think that there's strong stability in this rating," Yves LeMay told Reuters from New York.
He said Moody's was planning to visit New Zealand soon, but declined to specify the date.

"We have a policy of not providing specific dates publicly. All I can say is we do visit as part of our ongoing monitoring process at least once a year and...we do plan a visit in the not-too-distant future," LeMay said.
Last week, Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters told Reuters New Zealand deserved a ratings upgrade when the two ratings institutions, Moody's and Standard and Poor's, came visiting.
"We have got some good news to tell them. I expect their assessment to reflect the reality of an economy which is being soundly managed with healthy surpluses," Peters said.
LeMay said Moody's would spend several days in New Zealand to "take the pulse and discuss in detail the broad policy issues with government officials".
But he said New Zealand's present rating already reflected much of the economic restructuring of the past decade.

"Our view is that much of the progress that we've seen through the very extensive reform programmes implemented in the last 10 years are reflected in the ratings actions that we've taken in the last few years," he said.
"Two upgrades in the last three or four years -- that is a significant change."
Moody's last upgraded its New Zealand rating in February, 1996.
Last week, Standard and Poor's said its long-term foreign currency debt rating for New Zealand of AA+ was not expected to change over the next three years.
In contrast, Finance Minister Bill Birch said New Zealand's chances of achieving a return to a triple A credit rating were "higher than ever".
